name: Risk, Resilience and Incident Leadership
description: Risk identification, assessment and treatment, risk appetite, business continuity and disaster recovery, incident command and communication, blameless post-mortems, reliability targets, third-party risk, breach response, security governance, privacy, AI risk, key-person risk, insurance and regulatory change for leaders.

groups.treat: risk treatment option or control type

cards.subject: Risk
says: describes something uncertain that could affect an objective
combines a chance of happening with a consequence if it does
cards.use: need to name something uncertain that could hurt a goal
not: is a problem that has already happened and needs action now

cards.subject: Likelihood
says: estimates how probable it is that a risk event occurs
is rated on a scale such as rare to almost certain
cards.use: need to judge how probable a threat is
not: estimates how much damage the event would cause

cards.subject: Impact
says: estimates the size of the consequence if a risk event occurs
can be measured in money, downtime, harm to people or lost trust
cards.use: need to judge how bad a threat would be if it happened
not: estimates how often the event is expected to occur

cards.subject: Risk score
says: multiplies likelihood by impact to rank risks
lets very different risks be compared on one scale
can rank a rare disaster and a frequent nuisance the same
cards.use: need to decide which of many risks to look at first
not: proves how much money a risk will cost

cards.subject: Risk register
says: records each identified risk with its rating, owner and treatment
is reviewed on a regular schedule rather than filed once
becomes shelfware when no one is accountable for updating it
cards.use: need one shared list of known risks and who is handling each
not: is written once at project start and then closed

cards.subject: Risk owner
says: is the named person accountable for managing one risk
holds the authority to fund or decide its treatment
is a person or role, not a committee
cards.use: find a register entry that nobody is acting on
not: is always the security team regardless of the risk

cards.subject: Risk appetite
says: states how much risk the organisation is willing to pursue to meet its goals
is set by the board or executive leadership
guides which risks are worth taking in the first place
cards.use: need to decide whether a new venture's level of risk is acceptable in principle
not: is a measurable limit on one specific metric

cards.subject: Risk tolerance
says: sets the acceptable variation around one specific objective
is expressed as a measurable limit such as maximum hours of downtime
is narrower and more operational than appetite
cards.use: need a concrete threshold that triggers escalation
not: is the board's broad statement of strategy

cards.subject: Residual risk
says: is the risk that remains after controls and treatments are applied
is the level a named owner formally accepts when treatment is finished
is never exactly zero
cards.use: need to know what exposure is left after the controls are in place
not: is the risk before any control is counted

cards.subject: Key risk indicator
says: is a metric that signals rising exposure before a loss occurs
triggers escalation when it crosses an agreed threshold
cards.use: need an early warning that a risk is growing
not: counts the losses that already happened last year

cards.subject: Quantitative risk analysis
says: expresses risk as ranges of probable financial loss
uses estimated frequencies and loss sizes instead of colour ratings
needs calibrated estimates to avoid false precision
cards.use: must compare a security spend against the expected loss it prevents
not: removes the need for expert judgement

cards.subject: Risk velocity
says: measures how quickly a risk event reaches the business once it triggers
raises the priority of fast-moving risks that leave little time to respond
cards.use: find that a moderate risk would hit the business within minutes of starting
not: measures how often the event is expected to occur

cards.subject: Risk avoidance
says: stops the activity that creates the risk
gives up the potential benefit of that activity along with the risk
cards.use: decide a venture's exposure is beyond appetite and drop it
not: keeps the activity but adds extra controls

cards.subject: Risk mitigation
says: lowers likelihood, impact or both through controls
continues the activity while reducing exposure
leaves some residual risk behind
cards.use: can cut a risk with extra safeguards and still run the activity
not: shifts the cost of a loss to an insurer

cards.subject: Risk transfer
says: shifts the financial consequence to another party such as an insurer or supplier
leaves reputational harm with the organisation
cards.use: want a third party to bear the cost of a rare but severe loss
not: removes the underlying cause of the risk

cards.subject: Risk acceptance
says: knowingly keeps a risk without further treatment
needs a named owner's sign-off and a review date
cards.use: find that treating a risk would cost more than the loss it prevents
not: means a risk is ignored because nobody noticed it

cards.subject: Preventive control
says: stops a risk event from happening in the first place
is exemplified by access restrictions and approval steps
cards.use: want to block an unauthorised change before it takes effect
not: discovers an event after it has started

cards.subject: Detective control
says: discovers that an event has happened or is happening
depends on someone acting on the alert it raises
is exemplified by log review and monitoring
cards.use: want to be told when something slips past the barriers
not: restores systems after an event

cards.subject: Corrective control
says: limits damage and restores the normal state after an event
reduces impact rather than preventing the event
is exemplified by restoring from backup
cards.use: need to bring a damaged system back after a failure
not: blocks the event before it begins

cards.subject: Compensating control
says: stands in for a required control that cannot be implemented
must deliver a comparable level of protection
cards.use: cannot apply a mandated control because of a technical constraint
not: is any extra control added beyond what is required

cards.subject: Defence in depth
says: layers several independent controls so one failure is not fatal
avoids relying on a single safeguard
cards.use: worry that one failed safeguard could expose everything
not: relies on one very strong perimeter control

cards.subject: Business impact analysis
says: identifies critical processes and the cost of interrupting them over time
sets the recovery priorities that plans are built on
cards.use: need to know which services must come back first
not: tests whether a backup can be restored

cards.subject: Business continuity plan
says: keeps critical business functions running during a disruption
covers people, premises, suppliers and processes, not only IT
cards.use: need staff to keep serving customers while systems are down
not: restores servers and databases after a failure

cards.subject: Disaster recovery plan
says: restores IT systems and data after a major failure
usually forms one component of the wider continuity effort
cards.use: need step-by-step instructions to rebuild systems at another site
not: decides how staff work from home during a disruption

cards.subject: Recovery time objective
says: is the longest acceptable time to restore a service after an outage
drives how much to invest in redundancy and failover
cards.use: need to decide how fast a service must be back
not: is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time

cards.subject: Recovery point objective
says: is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time
sets how often backups or replication must run
cards.use: need to decide how much recent data the business can afford to lose
not: is the longest acceptable time to restore the service

cards.subject: Maximum tolerable period of disruption
says: is the point at which an outage threatens the survival of the organisation
sets an upper bound that the recovery time objective must stay inside
cards.use: need the outer limit beyond which the business itself would fail
not: is the data loss a service can accept

cards.subject: Active-active deployment
says: serves live traffic from more than one site at the same time
can give near-zero recovery time at the highest cost
cards.use: need that customers notice nothing when a whole site fails
not: keeps an idle environment that is built only after disaster

cards.subject: Warm standby
says: keeps a scaled-down copy running that is scaled up on failure
recovers in minutes to hours at moderate cost
cards.use: want faster recovery than rebuilding but cannot afford a full duplicate
not: provisions the environment only after a disaster is declared

cards.subject: Cold standby
says: provisions the environment only after a disaster is declared
is the cheapest option and the slowest to recover
cards.use: accept days of downtime for a low-priority system
not: serves live traffic from several sites at once

cards.subject: Failover
says: switches service to a standby component when the primary fails
can be automatic or a manual decision
cards.use: need service to move to the backup when the primary breaks
not: returns traffic to the original site after repair

cards.subject: Backup restore test
says: proves that a backup can actually be restored within the required time
reveals broken or incomplete backups before a disaster does
cards.use: learn that nobody has ever restored from the backups
not: counts how many backup jobs ran successfully

cards.subject: Immutable backup
says: cannot be altered or deleted for a set retention period
protects recovery from ransomware that targets backups
cards.use: worry that an attacker with admin rights could erase every backup copy
not: is any backup stored on the same server as the data

cards.subject: Single point of failure
says: is a component whose failure stops the whole service
is found by tracing the dependencies of a critical service
cards.use: need to find the one part that could take everything down
not: is a component that has several redundant copies

cards.subject: Incident commander
says: owns decisions and coordination for the duration of an incident
delegates hands-on fixing rather than debugging personally
decides when to escalate or declare the incident over
cards.use: need one person making the call while many people work an outage
not: writes the customer updates

cards.subject: Operations lead
says: directs the technical work of diagnosing and mitigating
reports findings and options to the incident commander
cards.use: need someone to run the technical investigation and keep engineers from duplicating effort
not: owns the final decision on severity

cards.subject: Communications lead
says: writes and sends updates to stakeholders and customers
shields responders from constant status questions
cards.use: need someone to keep stakeholders informed so responders can focus
not: records a timestamped log of every action

cards.subject: Scribe
says: records a timestamped log of actions and decisions during the incident
provides the raw timeline later used in the post-mortem
cards.use: need an accurate record of who did what and when
not: sends the customer status updates

cards.subject: Incident severity level
says: classifies an incident by its business impact
decides who is paged and how often updates go out
is defined in advance so nobody argues about it mid-incident
cards.use: need to decide how large a response an incident deserves
not: is chosen by whichever engineer finds the problem and never changed

cards.subject: Incident declaration
says: formally starts the response process and assigns roles
is better made early and downgraded than made late
cards.use: suspect customer impact but do not yet know the cause
not: waits until the root cause is confirmed

cards.subject: Escalation path
says: defines who is called next when the first responder cannot resolve the issue
includes time-based and severity-based triggers
cards.use: cannot reach the owner of a failing service and the clock is running
not: rates how serious an incident is

cards.subject: Mitigation before diagnosis
says: restores service first and investigates the cause afterwards
favours rollback or failover over live debugging
cards.use: can undo the last release to end customer impact while the cause is unknown
not: requires the root cause to be proven before any change

cards.subject: Runbook
says: gives step-by-step instructions for a known operational situation
reduces reliance on memory under stress
cards.use: want a tired on-call engineer to handle a known alert correctly
not: records the lessons of a past incident

cards.subject: Holding statement
says: acknowledges an issue while facts are still unclear
commits to a time for the next update
cards.use: must say something publicly before the cause is known
not: announces the final cause and the fix

cards.subject: Single spokesperson
says: speaks for the organisation during a crisis
prevents contradictory messages from different people
cards.use: see several leaders giving different accounts to the press
not: lets each team answer questions in its own words

cards.subject: Fixed update cadence
says: promises updates at set intervals even when nothing has changed
reduces inbound questions because people know when to expect news
cards.use: find stakeholders chasing responders for status every few minutes
not: sends an update only when the cause is known

cards.subject: Status page
says: publishes service health to customers in one known place
is hosted separately from the systems it reports on
cards.use: need customers to check service health without contacting support
not: is an internal log read only by responders

cards.subject: Customer impact statement
says: describes what customers can and cannot do right now
leads with the effect on users rather than the technical cause
cards.use: need to tell customers what is affected in plain words
not: explains the architecture of the failing component

cards.subject: Executive briefing
says: gives leaders the impact, current status, decisions needed and next update time
keeps executives out of the technical response channel
cards.use: need to update the CEO without interrupting the responders
not: contains the full engineering log for the CEO to read

cards.subject: Internal-first communication
says: tells employees before or together with the public
gives staff approved lines for customer questions
cards.use: worry that staff will learn about the crisis from the news
not: keeps staff uninformed to prevent leaks

cards.subject: Dark site
says: is a pre-built page held ready to publish in a crisis
does not depend on the primary website's infrastructure
cards.use: expect the main website to be down when you need to publish
not: is a hidden page used to collect customer complaints

cards.subject: Blameless post-mortem
says: examines how the system allowed the failure rather than who erred
assumes people acted sensibly on the information they had
encourages honest reporting of mistakes
cards.use: want people to share what really happened after an outage
not: names the person responsible and records a penalty

cards.subject: Incident timeline
says: orders events with timestamps from first impact to resolution
is built from the scribe's log, chat history and monitoring data
cards.use: need to reconstruct exactly what happened and when
not: lists the future improvements and their owners

cards.subject: Contributing-factor analysis
says: recognises that incidents usually have several causes that combined
replaces the search for a single culprit
cards.use: find that a failure needed three separate weaknesses to line up
not: stops once the first cause is found

cards.subject: Five whys
says: asks why repeatedly to move from symptom towards cause
can mislead by following one linear chain of reasoning
cards.use: want a quick technique for tracing a symptom back through the process
not: maps every factor that contributed in parallel

cards.subject: Action item
says: turns a lesson into a specific change with an owner and due date
is worthless unless tracked to completion
cards.use: need the post-mortem to produce real change
not: is a general intention to do better next time

cards.subject: Follow-through review
says: checks periodically that post-mortem actions were finished
reports overdue actions to leadership
cards.use: see the same incident repeat because earlier fixes were never completed
not: is held once, straight after the incident ends

cards.subject: Incident trend review
says: looks across many incidents for recurring themes
finds systemic weaknesses invisible in any single post-mortem
cards.use: suspect separate outages share an underlying pattern
not: checks that last month's action items are done

cards.subject: Near-miss review
says: learns from events that almost caused harm
depends on a culture where reporting is safe
cards.use: want to learn from a failure that was caught by luck
not: investigates only incidents that caused customer impact

cards.subject: Mean time to detect
says: measures the average time from start of impact until someone knows
improves with better monitoring and alerting
cards.use: want to know how long failures run unnoticed
not: measures the average time to restore service

cards.subject: Mean time to recover
says: measures the average time from start of an outage until service is restored
improves with rehearsed rollback and clear runbooks
cards.use: want to know how long outages typically last
not: measures how long failures run unnoticed

cards.subject: Hindsight bias
says: makes an outcome seem obvious once it is known
leads reviewers to judge earlier decisions unfairly
cards.use: notice reviewers saying the warning signs were plain to see
not: comes from reviewing too little data

cards.subject: Service level indicator
says: is a measured quantity describing service health such as request success rate
supplies the numbers that objectives are judged on
cards.use: need to decide what to measure about a service
not: is a promise to customers with penalties

cards.subject: Service level objective
says: sets the internal reliability goal for an indicator over a time window
guides engineering decisions about reliability work
cards.use: need an agreed target for how reliable a service should be
not: is a contract term that pays credits when missed

cards.subject: Service level agreement
says: is a contractual promise to customers
carries consequences such as credits when missed
cards.use: need to state in a contract what a customer is promised
not: is a purely internal engineering target

cards.subject: Error budget
says: is the amount of unreliability an objective allows over a window
equals 100 percent minus the objective
lets teams spend risk on shipping change
cards.use: need to balance feature speed against stability with a number
not: is the money set aside to pay SLA credits

cards.subject: Error budget policy
says: states what changes when the budget is spent, such as pausing feature releases
settles the response in advance so it is not argued during a crisis
cards.use: find teams disagreeing about whether to freeze releases after repeated outages
not: sets the target availability for a service

cards.subject: Burn rate
says: measures how fast the error budget is being consumed
supports alerts that fire on fast or slow depletion
cards.use: want to be warned that the budget will run out well before the window ends
not: is the total unreliability allowed in a window

cards.subject: Availability percentage
says: expresses uptime as a share such as 99.9 percent
cuts permitted downtime tenfold with each added nine
cards.use: need to translate a reliability target into allowed minutes of downtime
not: measures how quickly failures are detected

cards.subject: Symptom-based alerting
says: pages people on user-visible failures rather than internal causes
reduces noise from alerts nobody needs to act on
cards.use: find that on-call is flooded with alerts that never affect users
not: alerts on every metric that crosses a threshold

cards.subject: 100 percent reliability target
says: costs far more than it returns because users cannot perceive the difference
is unrealistic when dependencies fail more often than that
cards.use: hear a stakeholder demand that the service must never fail
not: is the sensible default for every critical service

cards.subject: Vendor tiering
says: ranks suppliers by data access and business criticality
decides how much due diligence each supplier receives
cards.use: have hundreds of suppliers and limited review capacity
not: gives every supplier an identical review

cards.subject: Security questionnaire
says: collects a vendor's self-reported control answers
needs evidence checking because answers are unverified
cards.use: need a first view of a supplier's security practices
not: independently tests the supplier's systems

cards.subject: Concentration risk
says: arises when too much depends on one supplier or region
turns a single provider outage into a company-wide one
cards.use: find that every critical service runs on the same cloud region
not: comes from having many small suppliers

cards.subject: Fourth-party risk
says: comes from the suppliers of your suppliers
stays invisible unless the contract requires disclosure of subprocessors
cards.use: discover your vendor relies on an unknown provider for your data
not: comes from your own direct employees

cards.subject: Software bill of materials
says: lists the components and libraries inside a software product
lets you check quickly whether a newly disclosed flaw affects you
cards.use: hear about a critical flaw in a common library and need to know where you use it
not: lists the licences you have bought

cards.subject: Supply-chain attack
says: compromises a trusted supplier or dependency to reach its customers
arrives through legitimate updates and so bypasses the perimeter
cards.use: learn that a trusted update was tampered with at its source
not: exploits a flaw in your own firewall

cards.subject: Exit plan
says: describes how to leave a vendor with data returned and service moved
is best agreed before signing, when leverage is greatest
cards.use: depend on one supplier and fear being trapped
not: is written after the vendor relationship has failed

cards.subject: Right to audit
says: lets the customer inspect or commission a review of a supplier's controls
is a contract clause rather than a technical control
cards.use: need to verify a critical supplier's claims beyond its questionnaire
not: lets the supplier audit the customer's staff

cards.subject: Source code escrow
says: deposits source code with a neutral party to be released on defined events
protects against supplier insolvency or abandonment of a product
cards.use: depend on a small vendor's software and fear it could vanish
not: lets the customer read the source at any time

cards.subject: Personal data breach
says: is a security incident that exposes personal data to unauthorised parties
includes accidental disclosure and loss, not only attacks
cards.use: find that a spreadsheet of customer records was emailed to the wrong recipient
not: happens only when an outside attacker steals data

cards.subject: Containment
says: stops a breach from spreading or continuing
comes before eradication and recovery
cards.use: must stop an attacker from reaching more systems right now
not: removes the attacker's access for good

cards.subject: Eradication
says: removes the attacker's access and malicious artefacts from the environment
must be complete or the attacker returns
cards.use: must make sure no backdoor remains after containing an intrusion
not: limits the attacker's movement in the short term

cards.subject: Evidence preservation
says: keeps logs and disk images intact for investigation
conflicts with the urge to wipe and rebuild immediately
cards.use: want to rebuild an infected server but need to keep forensic proof
not: deletes affected systems as fast as possible

cards.subject: Breach assessment
says: judges the likely harm to affected people from the exposed data
informs whether notification to authorities or individuals is required
cards.use: need to decide whether a leak must be reported
not: lists the controls that failed

cards.subject: Notification clock
says: is a regulator-set time limit that often runs from the moment of awareness
makes early escalation to legal and privacy staff essential
cards.use: suspect a breach on a Friday and wonder whether the weekend counts
not: starts only when the investigation is complete

cards.subject: Affected-person notification
says: tells the people whose data was exposed what happened and what to do
explains likely consequences and protective steps in plain language
cards.use: must write to customers whose data was exposed
not: is sent only to the regulator

cards.subject: Legal counsel engagement
says: brings lawyers in early to advise on obligations and on how findings are shared
helps keep investigation discussions deliberate and controlled
cards.use: face a breach with unclear notification duties
not: delays the response until the investigation ends

cards.subject: Ransom payment decision
says: is a leadership decision weighing legal limits, recovery options and uncertain outcomes
does not guarantee that stolen data is deleted or returned
cards.use: face encrypted systems and a demand for payment
not: is made by the IT team alone as a technical matter

cards.subject: ISO 27001
says: is an international standard for an information security management system
can be certified by an independent accredited auditor
requires continual improvement of the system
cards.use: need a certification recognised internationally across industries
not: is an audit report written about service organisations

cards.subject: SOC 2
says: is an independent auditor's report on a service organisation's controls
is built on the trust services criteria
is commonly requested by customers during supplier reviews
cards.use: hear a customer ask for an auditor's report on how you protect their data
not: is a certificate of a management system

cards.subject: Information security management system
says: is the set of policies, processes and roles that manage security systematically
runs on a plan, do, check, act cycle
cards.use: want security managed as an ongoing system rather than a project
not: is a single software tool that blocks attacks

cards.subject: Statement of applicability
says: lists which controls apply and why others are excluded
is a required document in ISO 27001 certification
cards.use: must justify why some standard controls are not used
not: lists the incidents of the past year

cards.subject: SOC 2 Type I
says: describes whether controls are suitably designed at one point in time
is quicker to obtain than a Type II report
cards.use: need a first report quickly and have no operating history yet
not: tests controls over a period of months

cards.subject: SOC 2 Type II
says: tests whether controls operated effectively over a period
gives customers stronger assurance than a point-in-time view
cards.use: need to show that controls worked consistently over time
not: describes control design at a single date

cards.subject: Information security policy
says: sets management's top-level security rules and intent
is approved by senior leadership and reviewed periodically
cards.use: need a rule that every employee must follow
not: is a technical procedure for configuring one server

cards.subject: Policy exception process
says: records a time-limited deviation from policy with an owner who accepts the risk
brings unofficial workarounds into view
cards.use: find a team that cannot comply with a policy for a good reason
not: approves permanent deviations without review

cards.subject: Security awareness training
says: teaches staff to recognise and report threats such as phishing
works best when repeated and reinforced regularly
cards.use: want staff to spot and report suspicious emails
not: replaces technical controls

cards.subject: Three lines model
says: separates management, risk oversight and independent assurance
keeps internal audit independent of the controls it checks
cards.use: find that the team running a control is also the one checking it
not: puts all risk work under one team

cards.subject: Segregation of duties
says: splits a sensitive task between people so one person cannot abuse it alone
is exemplified by separating who requests a payment from who approves it
cards.use: find one person can create and approve the same payment
not: gives one trusted person full control to speed things up

cards.subject: Board security reporting
says: translates technical status into risk, trend and decision terms
avoids raw vulnerability counts as the headline
cards.use: must brief directors who are not technical
not: lists every alert from the monitoring tools

cards.subject: Compliance-as-security fallacy
says: confuses a point-in-time audit result with ongoing security
assumes a certificate proves the organisation cannot be breached
cards.use: hear a leader say passing the audit means we are safe
not: recognises that audits replace security work

cards.subject: Data controller
says: decides why and how personal data is processed
carries primary accountability to individuals and regulators
cards.use: are the party that decides the purpose of collecting customer data
not: processes data only on another party's instructions

cards.subject: Data processor
says: processes personal data on behalf of a controller
acts on documented instructions
cards.use: are a supplier handling customer data only to provide a service
not: decides independently why the data is collected

cards.subject: Data subject
says: is the living individual that the personal data is about
holds rights such as access and correction
cards.use: need the term for the person whose data is held
not: is the organisation holding the data

cards.subject: Personal data
says: is any information relating to an identifiable person
includes indirect identifiers such as online identifiers
cards.use: are unsure whether a record counts as covered by privacy rules
not: covers only names and addresses

cards.subject: Lawful basis
says: is the justification required before personal data may be processed
must be identified before processing starts, not afterwards
cards.use: want to start a new use of customer data and must justify it
not: is always the individual's consent

cards.subject: Consent
says: is one lawful basis that must be freely given, specific and informed
must be as easy to withdraw as to give
cards.use: rely on the individual's agreement as the justification
not: can be assumed from silence or pre-ticked boxes

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: collects and keeps only the data needed for the stated purpose
limits exposure by holding less
cards.use: are asked to add a form field that is not needed for the service
not: keeps all data in case it is useful later

cards.subject: Data protection impact assessment
says: assesses privacy risks of high-risk processing before it starts
identifies measures that reduce harm to individuals
cards.use: plan a new system that profiles people on a large scale
not: is done after launch as a review

cards.subject: Privacy by design
says: builds privacy protections into systems from the start
defaults to the most protective setting
cards.use: are designing a new product and want privacy built in, not added later
not: adds protections after a complaint

cards.subject: Data subject access request
says: lets an individual ask for a copy of the data held about them
depends on knowing where personal data lives across systems
cards.use: receive a request from a customer for everything held about them
not: lets an authority inspect the company's servers

cards.subject: Pseudonymisation
says: replaces identifiers with a key held separately
still counts as personal data because re-identification is possible
cards.use: want analysts to work on data without seeing names while keeping the ability to re-link
not: makes data permanently non-personal

cards.subject: Anonymisation
says: removes identifiability irreversibly so data is no longer personal
is hard to achieve when datasets can be combined
cards.use: want to publish a dataset that can never be traced back to people
not: is achieved by replacing names with codes

cards.subject: Hallucination
says: is fluent model output that is false or unsupported
cannot be ruled out by a model's confident tone
cards.use: see a model cite a source that does not exist
not: is a deliberate attack on the model

cards.subject: Prompt injection
says: hides instructions in input that the model may follow as commands
is hard to block completely when models read untrusted content
cards.use: let an AI assistant read emails or web pages from outsiders
not: is false output caused by missing training data

cards.subject: Shadow AI
says: is staff use of unapproved AI tools with company data
grows when approved tools are slow or missing
cards.use: find employees pasting customer records into a free chatbot
not: is an approved assistant running in the background

cards.subject: AI acceptable use policy
says: states which AI tools, data and tasks are permitted
tells staff which data must never be put into external tools
cards.use: need clear rules for staff before rolling out AI tools
not: lists the technical architecture of the models

cards.subject: Human in the loop
says: places a person to review or approve high-impact outputs before they take effect
needs real authority, time and information to override
cards.use: let an AI recommend decisions that significantly affect individuals
not: means a person is told about the output afterwards

cards.subject: Automation bias
says: is the tendency to over-trust automated suggestions
can reduce a human-review control to a rubber stamp
cards.use: notice reviewers approve almost every AI suggestion without checking
not: is a model's skew against a demographic group

cards.subject: Model drift
says: is a decline in model performance as real-world data changes
is caught by monitoring quality over time
cards.use: see a once-accurate model slowly get worse as customer behaviour changes
not: is a model suddenly changed by its provider

cards.subject: AI use-case inventory
says: lists every AI system in use with its owner, data and purpose
is the base on which any governance depends
cards.use: cannot answer how many AI tools the company is using
not: lists the training datasets of one model

cards.subject: Risk-tiered AI governance
says: applies stronger review to higher-impact AI uses
avoids a heavy process for low-risk uses
cards.use: need to govern dozens of AI uses without blocking harmless ones
not: applies the same full review to every use

cards.subject: Vendor model change risk
says: arises when a provider updates a model so its behaviour shifts
is mitigated by version pinning and regression tests
cards.use: find outputs changed overnight though your own code did not
not: is caused by changing market data over months

cards.subject: Key-person risk
says: arises when critical knowledge or authority rests with one individual
is reduced by documentation, deputies and sharing responsibilities
cards.use: find that only one engineer knows how the billing system works
not: is solved by retaining the person with a bonus alone

cards.subject: Succession plan
says: names and prepares people to take over critical roles
covers both planned departures and sudden loss
cards.use: need to know who steps in if a senior leader leaves tomorrow
not: lists the current staff by seniority

cards.subject: Tabletop exercise
says: walks a team through a scenario by discussion without touching systems
exposes gaps in roles and decisions cheaply
cards.use: want to rehearse the response plan without disrupting production
not: injects real failures into running systems

cards.subject: Game day
says: injects real failures to rehearse response and test system behaviour
finds technical weaknesses that discussion would miss
cards.use: want to learn whether failover actually works under real faults
not: is a discussion-only walkthrough of a scenario

cards.subject: Scenario planning
says: explores several plausible futures and prepares options for each
does not try to predict the single most likely outcome
cards.use: face deep uncertainty where forecasting one outcome is unreliable
not: picks the most probable forecast and plans only for it

cards.subject: Pre-mortem
says: imagines the project has already failed and works backwards to find causes
surfaces concerns people hesitate to voice in planning
cards.use: want a team to name the ways a plan could fail before it starts
not: reviews a failure after it has happened

cards.subject: Graceful degradation
says: lets a service keep core functions when a dependency fails
trades full features for continued availability
cards.use: want the shop to keep taking orders even if recommendations break
not: shuts down the whole service when any part fails

cards.subject: Crisis management team
says: brings executives together with defined roles to lead the response to a major event
separates strategic decisions from the technical response
cards.use: face an event so serious that it needs executive decisions beyond the technical team
not: replaces the incident commander during the technical work

cards.subject: Cyber insurance
says: transfers part of the financial cost of cyber events to an insurer
does not replace controls and does not restore reputation
cards.use: want to cover the costs of response and recovery for a rare large loss
not: guarantees that the insurer prevents attacks

cards.subject: Policy retention
says: is the amount of a loss the insured pays before cover applies
is higher when the premium is lower
cards.use: must choose how much loss to bear before the insurer pays
not: is the maximum amount the insurer will pay

cards.subject: Policy exclusion
says: names circumstances the insurer will not cover
can remove cover for events such as unpatched known flaws or acts of war
cards.use: read a policy to learn what would not be paid
not: extends cover to additional events

cards.subject: Policy sublimit
says: caps cover for one type of loss below the overall limit
can leave a large gap for costs such as extortion or regulatory response
cards.use: find that the policy pays far less than expected for one kind of loss
not: is the amount the insured must pay first

cards.subject: Horizon scanning
says: looks ahead for emerging rules, technologies and threats
gives time to prepare before new obligations apply
cards.use: want early warning of regulation that will affect the business
not: checks compliance with rules already in force

cards.subject: Obligations register
says: lists the laws, contracts and standards the organisation must meet
links each obligation to an owner and the controls that satisfy it
cards.use: cannot say which rules apply to a product or who is responsible
not: lists the risks the board has accepted

cards.subject: Regulatory change impact assessment
says: analyses how a new or changed rule affects processes, systems and cost
produces an owned plan and date for any required change
cards.use: learn that a rule will change and need to know what must be altered
not: monitors for emerging rules

qa.q: A risk is rated likelihood 4 and impact 5 on a five-point scale. What is its score under the usual multiplication method?
qa.why: The usual score multiplies likelihood by impact, so 4 x 5 = 20.

qa.q: What is the main job of a risk register?
qa.right: To hold every identified risk with its rating, owner and treatment in one reviewed list
wrong: To log every incident after it has been resolved
To record the budget for each security tool
To replace the board's risk appetite statement
qa.why: A register is the living list of risks and who is managing each.

qa.q: What does a recovery point objective describe?
qa.right: How much recent data the business can afford to lose, measured in time
wrong: How long the service may stay down
How many staff must be on call
How often the disaster recovery plan is printed
qa.why: RPO is about data loss; RTO is about downtime.

qa.q: What does a recovery time objective describe?
qa.right: The longest acceptable time to bring a service back after an outage
wrong: The amount of data that may be lost
The time the post-mortem must be published
The number of backup copies to keep
qa.why: RTO is the downtime limit.

qa.q: What is the purpose of a blameless post-mortem?
qa.right: To learn how the system allowed the failure so it can be improved
wrong: To decide which person should be disciplined
To prove to customers the company did nothing wrong
To produce the record needed for insurance only
qa.why: Blamelessness encourages honest accounts, which is what makes learning possible.

qa.q: Which statement best separates an SLO from an SLA?
qa.right: An SLO is an internal reliability goal, while an SLA is a contractual promise with consequences
wrong: An SLO is for databases and an SLA is for web servers
An SLO is measured yearly and an SLA monthly
An SLO is written by customers and an SLA by engineers
qa.why: Teams typically set the SLO stricter than the SLA so they have room to react before breaking the contract.

qa.q: A service has a 99.9 percent monthly availability objective. What is the error budget?
qa.right: 0.1 percent of the month's requests or time
wrong: 99.9 percent of the month
1 percent of the month
The number of incidents allowed per year
qa.why: The budget is 100 percent minus the objective.

qa.q: Which statement about the three roles of controls is correct?
qa.right: Preventive controls block events, detective controls find them, corrective controls reduce damage afterwards
wrong: Detective controls block events, preventive controls find them
Corrective controls are applied before an event to reduce likelihood
All three do exactly the same job at different cost
qa.why: The three types act before, during and after an event.

qa.q: Under which circumstance is risk acceptance appropriate?
qa.right: The cost of treating the risk exceeds the expected loss and a named owner signs it off
wrong: The risk has not yet been assessed
The risk is hard to understand
The team cannot agree on a rating
qa.why: Acceptance must be a deliberate, recorded decision, not neglect.

qa.q: What does a business impact analysis produce that a disaster recovery plan depends on?
qa.right: The recovery priorities and time limits for each critical process
wrong: The list of staff to be dismissed after an event
The insurance premium for the year
The price of the backup tool
qa.why: BIA tells the plan what to recover first and how fast.

qa.q: What distinguishes a fixed update cadence in incident communication?
qa.right: It promises updates at set intervals even when there is nothing new
wrong: It sends an update only when the cause is confirmed
It lets each responder post whenever convenient
It replaces the status page
qa.why: Predictable updates reduce interruptions and anxiety.

qa.q: In privacy terms, which party decides why and how personal data is processed?
qa.right: The controller
wrong: The processor
The data subject
The auditor
qa.why: The controller decides purposes and means; a processor acts on its instructions.

qa.q: What is the difference between risk appetite and risk tolerance?
qa.right: Appetite is the broad level of risk leadership will pursue, tolerance is a measurable limit for one objective
wrong: Appetite is for security risks and tolerance for financial risks
Appetite is set by staff and tolerance by the board
They are two names for the same threshold
qa.why: Tolerance turns appetite into concrete limits that trigger escalation.

qa.q: Why do teams run backup restore tests?
qa.right: A backup that has never been restored is an assumption, not a capability
wrong: Restore tests lower the cost of storage
Restore tests are required to keep backup software licensed
They remove the need for an RPO
qa.why: Only a test shows backups are complete and restorable within the RTO.

qa.q: What is the strongest reason to use mitigation before diagnosis during an outage?
qa.right: Customer impact ends sooner, and the cause can be studied afterwards
wrong: The cause is rarely worth knowing
It avoids writing a post-mortem
Rollbacks never carry any risk
qa.why: Restoring service is the priority; root cause analysis can follow safely.

qa.q: What does SOC 2 Type II give a customer that Type I does not?
qa.right: Evidence that controls operated effectively over a period
wrong: A guarantee that the supplier will never be breached
Certification under an international standard
A list of the supplier's customers
qa.why: Type I describes design at one point in time; Type II tests operation over time.

qa.q: What makes a post-mortem action item useful?
qa.right: It names a specific change, an owner and a due date
wrong: It states a general wish for better care
It is assigned to the whole team
It is written only for incidents of the highest severity
qa.why: Without an owner and date, actions rarely happen.

qa.q: Which feature makes pseudonymised data still personal data?
qa.right: The key allowing re-identification still exists
wrong: It contains numbers
It is stored in the cloud
It has been shared with an employee
qa.why: If identity can be restored, the data remains personal.

qa.q: What is the main weakness of the five whys technique in a complex outage?
qa.right: It follows one linear chain and can miss other contributing factors
wrong: It requires an external facilitator
It cannot be applied after a customer complaint
It always names a person as the cause
qa.why: Complex failures have multiple causes; a single chain oversimplifies.

qa.q: Why is a software bill of materials valuable when a flaw in a common library is announced?
qa.right: It tells you quickly which of your products include the library
wrong: It patches the library automatically
It proves the library is safe
It removes the need for an exit plan
qa.why: The inventory turns a question of days into a lookup.

qa.q: What does human in the loop require to be a real control?
qa.right: Reviewers with authority, time and information to override the output
wrong: Someone being informed after the decision took effect
A reviewer who approves any output within seconds
A written policy mentioning review
qa.why: Without genuine ability to override, review becomes a formality.

qa.q: Which scenario describes concentration risk?
qa.right: All critical systems depend on one provider's single region
wrong: The company has many small suppliers
A vendor adds a new subprocessor
The company buys cyber insurance
qa.why: Dependence on one supplier or location turns one failure into a company-wide event.

qa.q: Why is a 100 percent reliability target usually a poor choice?
qa.right: The cost rises steeply and users cannot perceive the difference beyond their own dependencies
wrong: Regulators ban it
It prevents any error budget from being measured in percent
It requires too many staff to be on call at once
qa.why: Each extra nine costs more while returning less user value.

qa.q: An error budget policy is most useful for which purpose?
qa.right: Deciding in advance what happens, such as a release freeze, when the budget is spent
wrong: Setting the price of customer credits
Choosing the monitoring vendor
Assigning blame for outages
qa.why: A pre-agreed response removes argument at the moment of conflict.

qa.q: Why is immutable backup valuable against ransomware?
qa.right: Attackers with admin rights cannot erase the copies during the retention period
wrong: It makes backups restore faster
It removes the need to test restores
It encrypts the live data
qa.why: Immutability protects the last line of recovery.

qa.q: What is the main trade-off of an active-active deployment?
qa.right: Near-zero recovery time at the highest cost and complexity
wrong: It is cheap but slow to recover
It cannot survive a site failure
It needs no testing
qa.why: Running several live sites costs more, and data consistency is harder.

qa.q: Which approach reduces the risk of insurance exclusions leaving a gap?
qa.right: Read the exclusions and sublimits against your actual scenarios before buying
wrong: Choose the policy with the lowest premium
Assume the headline limit applies to every loss
Let the insurer define your risk appetite
qa.why: Cover is defined by its exclusions and sublimits, not the headline limit.

qa.q: What does a three lines model protect?
qa.right: Independence of assurance from the people who run the controls
wrong: The speed of software releases
The confidentiality of the register
The security budget
qa.why: Audit should not check its own work.

qa.q: Which statement about cyber insurance and risk transfer is most accurate?
qa.right: Insurance can cover some financial costs but does not remove the risk or the reputational damage
wrong: It transfers all liability to the insurer
It makes controls unnecessary
It guarantees the cover during any event
qa.why: Transfer shifts cost, not accountability or trust.

qa.q: Why does hindsight bias matter in a post-mortem?
qa.right: It makes past decisions look obviously wrong and discourages honest accounts
wrong: It makes incidents appear shorter
It hides the timeline
It causes more incidents
qa.why: Reviewers must reconstruct what responders knew at the time.

qa.q: What is the key weakness of treating compliance as proof of security?
qa.right: An audit is a point-in-time check against a standard, not proof against current threats
wrong: Audits are always dishonest
Standards forbid good security
Compliance costs too much
qa.why: Certificates show a baseline, not ongoing protection.

qa.q: A customer reports checkout failures at 02:10 and the on-call engineer cannot tell how widespread it is. What should happen first?
qa.right: Declare an incident at a provisional severity, assign an incident commander and open the incident channel
wrong: Wait until the cause is known before declaring
Email all customers an apology
Ask the CEO to approve the severity before paging anyone
qa.why: Early declaration with downgrade later is better than late declaration.

qa.q: Midway through a major outage the CTO joins the incident channel and starts giving engineering instructions. What is the best response from the incident commander?
qa.right: Brief the CTO and invite them to advise through the commander, keeping one voice of command
wrong: Let the CTO take over silently
Ask the CTO to leave the company channel
Pause the response until the CTO has read the logs
qa.why: Single command prevents conflicting orders; senior people can still contribute through the commander.

qa.q: Errors began right after the latest release and customers are affected, but the team wants more time to find the exact bug. What should the commander do?
qa.right: Roll back first, then diagnose from the preserved evidence
wrong: Keep debugging live until the bug is found
Disable monitoring to cut alert noise
Wait for the next scheduled release
qa.why: Mitigate first when a safe rollback exists and impact continues.

qa.q: The executive team asks for updates every ten minutes and is interrupting the responders. What should you do?
qa.right: Agree a fixed update cadence and have the communications lead brief them outside the technical channel
wrong: Tell executives to stop asking
Let engineers answer in the technical thread
Stop updating until the cause is found
qa.why: A predictable cadence meets the need without disturbing the work.

qa.q: A major customer posts about an outage on social media before the cause is known. What should the company say?
qa.right: Acknowledge the issue, describe what customers are experiencing and promise the next update time
wrong: Say nothing until the cause is confirmed
Blame the cloud supplier
Deny that anything is wrong until verified
qa.why: A holding statement fills the vacuum without guessing.

qa.q: After a breach is suspected on Friday evening, a manager says the team will decide on Monday whether it counts. What is the main concern?
qa.right: Notification time limits may already be running from the moment of awareness
wrong: Staff should not work over the weekend
The press may call on Monday
The cause is too uncertain to discuss
qa.why: Delays can consume regulatory time; legal and privacy staff need to know at once.

qa.q: A server holding customer data shows signs of intrusion. The engineer wants to wipe and rebuild immediately. What should the lead do?
qa.right: Contain the host and preserve images and logs first, then rebuild
wrong: Allow the rebuild to restore service sooner
Shut down logging to protect data
Delete the affected accounts quickly
qa.why: Evidence is needed to scope the breach and meet obligations.

qa.q: Attackers encrypt production systems and demand payment. Backups are partly affected. Who should make the decision on paying?
qa.right: Senior leadership with legal counsel, weighing legal limits and recovery options
wrong: The IT team on technical grounds
The first responder who found the note
The insurer without company input
qa.why: The decision has legal, financial and ethical dimensions beyond IT.

qa.q: Your post-mortem list from last quarter shows most action items open and the same outage has recurred. What should leadership do first?
qa.right: Establish a follow-through review with owners, dates and reporting of overdue actions
wrong: Ask the team to write fewer actions
Hold a new post-mortem with a different facilitator
Treat the repeat as unlucky
qa.why: Without follow-through, learning does not turn into change.

qa.q: A post-mortem draft concludes that an engineer made an error and recommends retraining them. What is the better response?
qa.right: Ask why the system allowed one slip to cause an outage and list the contributing factors
wrong: Accept the finding as the root cause
Remove the engineer from on-call
Delete the draft and move on
qa.why: Human error is a starting point for analysis, not its end.

qa.q: A supplier's security questionnaire is returned with every answer ticked yes. What is the best next step for a critical vendor?
qa.right: Request supporting evidence such as an audit report and verify key claims
wrong: Accept it since all answers are positive
Reject the vendor automatically
Send the same questionnaire again
qa.why: Self-reported answers need evidence, especially for critical vendors.

qa.q: A critical supplier tells you its own provider has been breached. Your contract has no clause for this. What should you do first?
qa.right: Ask what of your data is affected and start your own breach assessment
wrong: Wait for the supplier to finish its report
Terminate the contract immediately
Ignore it as the supplier's concern
qa.why: As the data owner you must assess impact even when the incident is upstream.

qa.q: A product team plans to feed customer support transcripts into an external AI tool. What should you do before approving?
qa.right: Check the provider's data handling terms and assess the privacy risks
wrong: Approve because the tool is popular
Ban all AI tools
Only ask the vendor to confirm in an email it is secure
qa.why: Data protection review and contract terms come before use.

qa.q: Employees paste confidential documents into a free chatbot because the approved tool is slow. What is the best leadership response?
qa.right: Fix the approved option and set clear rules, instead of relying on a ban alone
wrong: Block all AI sites and consider it solved
Ignore it unless data leaks
Punish the heaviest users publicly
qa.why: Shadow AI grows where sanctioned options fail to meet needs.

qa.q: A model's answers changed overnight though your code did not. The provider released an update. What should you do?
qa.right: Pin the model version where possible and run regression tests before accepting the change
wrong: Retrain the model on your own
Ignore the change since it is better
Switch to another provider at once
qa.why: Vendor changes are a known risk to be tested and controlled.

qa.q: Only one engineer understands the billing system and has just resigned. What should you do first?
qa.right: Capture knowledge with a handover, documentation and a named deputy before they leave
wrong: Offer a counter-offer and do nothing else
Wait until a problem occurs
Rewrite the system from scratch
qa.why: Key-person risk is reduced by sharing knowledge and responsibility.

qa.q: The CEO asks why the company still has unpatched legacy systems. The cost to retire them is high. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Present the risk in terms of likelihood, impact and cost, and ask a named owner to accept or fund it
wrong: Say it is a technical matter
Promise to fix everything this quarter
Hide the systems from the register
qa.why: Executives decide trade-offs when risks are presented in business terms with an owner.

qa.q: Your annual disaster recovery test shows a four-hour recovery for a service with a one-hour RTO. What should you do?
qa.right: Report the gap to the risk owner and decide whether to invest or accept the risk with sign-off
wrong: Change the RTO to match the result quietly
Wait for the next scheduled test
Mark the test as passed
qa.why: A gap is a risk decision, not an administrative detail.

qa.q: Two risks in the register share the same dependency on one data centre. How should you treat them?
qa.right: Recognise the correlation and assess the combined exposure of a single failure
wrong: Add the scores to get a total of independent risks
Delete one as a duplicate
Lower both scores because they are shared
qa.why: Correlated risks can fail together and so understate the aggregate.

qa.q: A new vendor will process personal data for you. Which document sets the vendor's handling obligations?
qa.right: A data processing agreement
wrong: A press release
A software bill of materials
A post-mortem report
qa.why: The agreement binds the processor to act on instructions and protect the data.

qa.q: A regulator announces a rule change that will affect how you store data in a year. What is the first step?
qa.right: Assess its impact, assign an owner and plan the changes
wrong: Wait until the deadline
Ask customers what they think
Update the risk appetite statement
qa.why: An owned impact assessment turns news into a plan.

qa.q: Your cyber insurance renewal asks for proof of multi-factor authentication and backups tested. What does this tell you?
qa.right: Insurers price cover on the controls you operate, so weak controls can raise cost or limit cover
wrong: Insurance now replaces those controls
The questions are only for marketing
Controls are optional for insured companies
qa.why: Underwriting links premiums and terms to controls.

qa.q: A customer asks for everything the company holds about them. What is this called?
qa.right: A data subject access request
wrong: A breach notification
A privacy impact assessment
A service level agreement
qa.why: Individuals can ask to see the data held about them.

qa.q: A team missed its SLO twice and has spent the error budget, but product pushes a feature launch. What does a good policy say?
qa.right: Pause non-essential feature releases until reliability work restores the budget
wrong: Launch anyway to keep customers
Raise the SLO target
Stop measuring reliability
qa.why: An error budget policy decides the trade-off in advance.

qa.q: The board receives a security report of 3,000 unpatched vulnerabilities. What is the better way to report?
qa.right: Show trend, risk to critical services and decisions needed from the board
wrong: Add the list as an appendix
Avoid reporting until the count falls
Show only good news
qa.why: The board needs risk and decisions, not raw counts.

qa.q: Which action is best at the start of a ransomware incident?
qa.right: Isolate affected systems to contain the spread and notify the incident commander
wrong: Delete all backups to be safe
Pay the ransom at once
Post details on social media
qa.why: Containment limits further damage while leadership decides next steps.

qa.q: Before a launch the team runs an exercise imagining it has failed badly a year from now. What is this called and what is its benefit?
qa.right: A pre-mortem, which surfaces concerns that planning meetings suppress
wrong: A post-mortem, which finds who was at fault
A game day, which tests failover under real faults
A tabletop exercise, which replays last year's outage
qa.why: Imagining failure in advance gives permission to voice doubts.

qa.q: You are asked to rank two risks of equal score: one rare but catastrophic, one frequent and minor. What additional factor deserves attention?
qa.right: How quickly each could reach the business and whether the catastrophic one threatens survival
wrong: The age of the risk entries
Which has the longer description
Which team raised it
qa.why: Equal scores can hide differences in speed and survivability.
